content: In HIV-infected individuals living in areas with a high prevalence of tuberculosis (TB), negative tuberculin skin test (TST) results are often false negatives, particularly in those with lower CD4 counts. The incidence of TB in the first six months after initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) is approximately 2 cases per 100 person-years (Kirenga et al., 2013). The BOTUSA trial (Samandari et al., 2011) provided data on TB incidence based on the duration of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) and ART. Among TST-positive individuals, 36 months of IPT reduced TB incidence by an additional 46% compared to six months of IPT in those receiving 360 days of ART. Specifically, TB incidence was reduced by 50% with six months of IPT and by 96% with 36 months of IPT, both compared to a group receiving no ART and six months of IPT. Conversely, in TST-negative individuals, 36 months of IPT only provided a 4% additional reduction in TB incidence on top of the 50% reduction achieved by ART and six months of IPT. In this group, TB incidence was reduced by 50% with six months of IPT and by 54% with 36 months of IPT, both compared to a group receiving no ART and six months of IPT (Rangaka et al., 2014). These findings suggest that longer-term IPT offers significant additional benefits for people living with HIV who are receiving ART in high TB-incidence settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends providing 36 months of IPT to adults and adolescents living with HIV in resource-constrained settings with high TB and HIV prevalence. Implementation of long-term IPT should be prioritized in high TB burden settings, such as those included in the systematic review (e.g., India, Botswana, South Africa). In moderate TB incidence settings, six months of IPT may be sufficient to prevent TB in HIV-infected individuals. For example, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, a medium TB burden setting, six months of IPT in TST-positive HIV-infected individuals was effective in preventing TB for up to seven years after cessation of IPT. Although there was an initial increase in TB risk immediately after stopping IPT, no increase was observed over the seven-year follow-up period (Golub et al., 2014). Monitoring and evaluation of IPT programs are essential to determine the applicability of revised recommendations for 36 months of IPT in people living with HIV. Research priorities include developing new point-of-care tests to identify active TB, latent TB infection, and uninfected individuals, with a focus on diagnostics for children. The role of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) in HIV-infected individuals with or without active TB should be further studied, particularly in relation to immune status. The use of TST in HIV-infected individuals receiving ART should also be evaluated, including the frequency of TST to assess immune reconstitution or boosting in those initially TST-negative. Preventive treatment for TB in HIV-infected individuals requires further research to evaluate the benefits and harms of rifamycin-containing regimens in resource-limited settings with high HIV and TB prevalence. Fixed-dose combinations of isoniazid, vitamin B6, and co-trimoxazole with antiretrovirals should be developed and assessed for efficacy and effectiveness. The feasibility and efficacy of long-term IPT in HIV-positive children and individuals co-infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) should also be studied. Optimal timing for initiating long-term IPT in relation to ART initiation needs to be determined, as well as the potential value of discontinuing lifelong IPT after immune reconstitution. Modeling studies should estimate the risks and benefits of long-term IPT, considering factors such as HIV and TB incidence, immune status, ART impact, IPT duration, and drug resistance prevalence. Operational research should address potential limitations of long-term IPT in populations with high isoniazid-resistant TB prevalence. The risks and benefits of administering isoniazid to undiagnosed individuals with active TB should be evaluated. The effectiveness of long-term IPT programs in resource-limited settings should be assessed, including cost-effectiveness and cost-benefit analyses from the perspectives of health systems and patients. Special populations, such as healthcare workers living with HIV, TST-negative healthcare workers, and HIV-exposed children, should be studied to determine the benefits and optimal duration of IPT. Population-based drug resistance surveillance is necessary to evaluate the impact of long-term IPT programs on community-level drug-resistant TB, including mono-isoniazid, mono-rifampicin, and multidrug-resistant TB. Ensuring optimal delivery of long-term IPT and other HIV care for women and children is also critical. The WHO's recommendation for 36 months of IPT in resource-constrained, high TB and HIV prevalence settings is based on evidence graded using the GRADE system. This system evaluates the certainty of evidence, with ratings ranging from high (indicating a very good indication of the likely effect) to very low (indicating unreliable evidence). The GRADE approach provides a transparent and systematic method for assessing the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations, which has been adopted by many international organizations.
